records.title: Section 56(2)(viib) ('angel tax') switched off from AY 2025-26
records.summary: The memorandum to the Finance (No. 2) Bill, 2024 says section 56(2)(viib), which taxed share premium above fair market value received by closely held companies, would not apply from assessment year 2025-26, effective 1 April 2025. The 23 July 2024 Budget speech announced abolishing 'angel tax' for all classes of investors. DPIIT's May 2026 tax playbook states angel tax was abolished with effect from 1 April 2025.

records.title: CCPS and CCDs as equity instruments under FEMA
records.summary: RBI's Master Direction treats preference shares and debentures as equity instruments for foreign investment only if fully paid and fully, compulsorily and mandatorily convertible. Optionally or partly convertible preference shares or debentures are debt and must follow External Commercial Borrowing rules. Equity instruments may carry an optionality clause with at least a one-year lock-in but no right to exit at an assured price. Treelife notes CCDs, unlike convertible notes, can be issued by any private company.
records.disclaimer: Not legal or tax advice — confirm with your CA / counsel.

records.title: Conversion pricing for CCPS and CCDs issued to non-residents
records.summary: For CCPS and CCDs held by non-residents, the price or conversion formula must be fixed at issue, and the conversion price cannot be lower than fair value worked out at issuance under the NDI Rules. Tenor amendments must comply with the Companies Act, 2013. Share warrants likewise need upfront pricing, with at least 25% of consideration paid upfront and the balance within 18 months.

records.title: Companies Act basics for issuing CCPS
records.summary: The Companies Act, 2013 allows only equity and preference share capital (section 43), bars irredeemable preference shares and permits redemption within up to 20 years (section 55). Treelife states CCPS are usually issued by private placement under section 42: an offer letter in Form PAS-4, a shareholder resolution, and a return of allotment in Form PAS-3 within 30 days, with a registered valuer's report for private placements.

records.title: Delaware corporations: domicile statistics and annual franchise tax
records.summary: Delaware's Division of Corporations says over 2 million entities and more than 66% of the Fortune 500 are Delaware-domiciled. records.title: Floor price for shares of an unlisted Indian company issued to non-residents
records.summary: NDI Rule 21 sets the issue price of an unlisted Indian company's equity instruments to a non-resident at not less than a valuation under any internationally accepted pricing methodology on an arm's-length basis, certified by a Chartered Accountant, SEBI-registered Merchant Banker or practising Cost Accountant. RBI's Master Direction adds that the valuation certificate must be at most 90 days old on the investment date. Pricing rules do not apply to non-repatriation investments.

records.title: Pricing for convertibles, transfers and swaps under FEMA
records.summary: For convertible instruments, the price or conversion formula must be fixed at issue and the conversion price cannot be below fair value worked out at issuance. Swaps need valuation by a SEBI-registered merchant banker or a regulated overseas investment banker, irrespective of amount.

records.title: Convertible notes: who may issue them to non-residents
records.summary: Under the NDI Rules, a convertible note is issued by a 'startup company': a private company under the Companies Act, 2013 identified as a startup under DPIIT notification G.S.R. 127(E) of 19 February 2019, as amended. It evidences money received as debt, repayable at the holder's option or convertible into equity within ten years on specified events. Startups in sectors needing government approval for foreign investment need that approval to issue notes to non-residents.

records.title: Convertible notes: minimum ticket, tenure and conversion
records.summary: A non-resident, other than Pakistani or Bangladeshi citizens or entities, may buy a startup's convertible notes for ₹25 lakh or more in a single tranche. RBI says notes were permitted from 10 January 2017. Treelife says the same ₹25 lakh single-tranche test applies to the deposit-rules exemption for domestic notes.

records.title: DPIIT startup definition revised in February 2026
records.summary: DPIIT notification G.S.R. 108(E) of 4 February 2026 supersedes G.S.R. 127(E) of 2019. The NDI Rules text on RBI's site (updated 2 September 2026) still cites G.S.R. 127(E) 'as amended'. Treelife's 2026 explainer still cites the older ₹100 crore limit.

records.summary: Treelife (June 2026) describes three routes: a direct share swap, where shareholders exchange Indian-company shares for shares of the overseas parent so it owns 100% of the Indian company; gradual migration, where the parent sets up a new Indian subsidiary and business moves across over time; and split-economics structures for later-stage companies. YC says flipped companies usually keep the original entity as an operating subsidiary of the new parent.

records.title: Overseas Investment Rules 2022: limits on resident individuals holding a foreign parent
records.summary: Under the FEMA (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022 (G.S.R. 646(E), 22 August 2022), a resident individual's overseas investment counts against the Liberalised Remittance Scheme ceiling. ODI is permitted only in an operating foreign entity, not in financial services, that has no subsidiary or step-down subsidiary where the individual has control; control includes rights to 10% or more of voting rights. Swaps arising from merger, demerger, amalgamation or liquidation are separately permitted. Rule 19(3) bars structures exceeding two layers of subsidiaries.
records.disclaimer: Not legal or tax advice — confirm with your CA / counsel.

records.title: FEMA treatment of share swaps into a new or existing foreign parent
records.summary: RBI's FDI Master Direction permits resident-to-non-resident transfers of Indian-company shares by swap for equity capital of a foreign company, subject to the OI Rules and any government approval. Swap valuation needs a SEBI-registered merchant banker or regulated overseas investment banker, whatever the amount. RBI's OI Master Direction requires both legs to comply with FEMA; equity acquired by swap that breaches the OI Rules, e.g. in a foreign entity with a subsidiary, must be sold within six months.

records.title: Indian tax consequences of a share-swap flip
records.summary: Treelife states that resident founders swapping Indian-company shares for foreign-parent shares make a transfer for capital-gains purposes, with gain equal to the fair value of parent shares received minus cost. The Income-tax Act, 1961 exemptions it cites are amalgamation-based and rarely fit a typical forward flip; otherwise it cites 12.5% long-term gains tax for unlisted shares held over 24 months. It also flags GAAR, POEM and transfer-pricing exposure after a flip.

records.title: iSAFE: origin and legal form (CCPS)
records.summary: 100X.VC says it pioneered the iSAFE (India Simple Agreement for Future Equity) in July 2019. An investor pays cash for a convertible security that legally takes the form of compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS), so authorised and paid-up capital rise by the amount invested. Templates cover valuation cap with discount, cap only, discount only and MFN. Holders get liquidation preference up to invested capital over founders and equity holders.

records.title: Why a US-style SAFE cannot take foreign investment into an Indian company
records.summary: Treelife states a US-style SAFE is a contractual right that is neither debt nor an eligible equity instrument under the NDI Rules, so foreign money cannot be received against it, whereas an iSAFE issued as CCPS can. RBI's Master Direction lists the equity instruments for foreign investment as equity shares, fully and mandatorily convertible debentures and preference shares, and share warrants. CCPS issued to non-residents must meet FEMA pricing and reporting.

records.title: Legal route: inbound cross-border merger under FEMA
records.summary: RBI's FEMA (Cross Border Merger) Regulations, 2018 let the Indian resultant company in an inbound merger issue securities to non-residents under FDI pricing, entry-route and reporting rules, and deem compliant transactions RBI-approved. An amendment effective 5 June 2026 replaced 'NCLT' with any 'Competent Authority' empowered under the Companies Act. Treelife and an Economic Times column report a September 2024 MCA change letting a foreign holding company merge into its Indian wholly-owned subsidiary by the fast-track route.
